analysis.one_liner: Gives federal tax credits of up to $4,500 to people and $100,000 to companies that donate to private school scholarship funds for low-income students.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in January 2017 with no cosponsors, sat in the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal income tax credit for donations to 'scholarship granting organizations' — nonprofits that exist solely to hand out tuition scholarships for elementary and secondary school. Only students from households earning up to 250% of the federal poverty line would be eligible, and the money could only go to schools that charge tuition, follow state law including anti-discrimination rules, and report student test results. Individuals could claim up to $4,500 in credits and corporations up to $100,000, and organizations would have to distribute at least 90% of their receipts each year or pay a 15% penalty tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families whose children could use scholarships to attend private K-12 schools they otherwise could not afford, and the donors — individuals and corporations — who would reduce their tax bills dollar-for-dollar for contributions. Private schools that charge tuition would gain paying students paid for by other taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit, up to $4,500 per individual taxpayer, for contributions to nonprofits that provide K-12 private school scholarships to students from low-income households.
Limits eligibility to students from households with income not exceeding 250% of the federal poverty guidelines, targeting the benefit to lower-income families.
Allows corporations a tax credit of up to $100,000 for the same kind of contributions, encouraging larger donations to the scholarship funds.

Requires participating schools to comply with state anti-discrimination, health and safety, and background-check laws, and to report student test results and achievement data to parents and to the Institute of Education Sciences for annual public evaluations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through the lost revenue from dollar-for-dollar tax credits for private donations. Money that would otherwise flow to the Treasury is redirected to private school tuition, and public schools could lose enrolled students and the per-pupil attention that follows them.

drawbacks.text: The credits are dollar-for-dollar reductions in tax owed, so every contributed dollar is a dollar less in federal revenue — with no official estimate in the record of what this would cost the Treasury.

The bill subsidizes private schools that charge tuition while excluding free public education: it expressly provides that scholarships cannot fund any school's obligation to provide a free, appropriate public education, shifting money toward the private sector.

Because eligibility depends on voluntary donations channeled through scholarship organizations, the benefit is not guaranteed for any student and depends on where donors and organizations choose to give.
Corporate and individual donors get their money back through tax credits, meaning taxpayers as a group finance contributions even when the donations would have happened anyway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give some low-income families real private school options they could not otherwise afford, and it includes more accountability than many private school choice programs: state anti-discrimination compliance, audits of the scholarship organizations, a 90% distribution requirement with a 15% penalty, and annual public evaluations of student outcomes. The honest cost is that the Treasury gives up a dollar of revenue for every donated dollar, and the aid reaches only the students that donor-funded organizations choose to help — a benefit that competes with, rather than strengthens, the public school system those students would otherwise attend.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Rubio introduced the bill in January 2017, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 17, 2017 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
The full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor consideration — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit, but the Treasury kept the revenue the credits would have cost, and public schools were spared the enrollment and funding pressure the scholarship program could have created. Private schools and their prospective donors simply did not get the new federal subsidy they would have received had it passed.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Educational Opportunities Act on January 17, 2017, creating tax credits for donations to private school scholarship organizations.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in January 2017 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a single cosponsor, so no party split on it was ever recorded; it was a Republican-sponsored measure that never moved past committee referral.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools that charge tuition
industries.note: The bill would have created a federally subsidized stream of tuition-paying scholarship students, but only for schools that charge tuition, comply with state anti-discrimination and safety laws, and report test results. The benefit flows to low-income families through the schools rather than to the schools directly.

The bill would have made these nonprofits the permanent mandatory channel for all federal education scholarships under the credit, with audits, income verification, and a 15% penalty for failing to distribute 90% of receipts. It would have created a new class of tax-advantaged intermediaries between taxpayers and schools.

Scholarships would have let low-income students leave for tuition-charging schools, and the tax credits would have drained federal revenue that could otherwise support public education. The bill expressly excludes using scholarships to fund public schools' obligation to provide a free, appropriate public education.

A dollar-for-dollar tax credit — up to $4,500 for individuals and $100,000 for corporations — means contributors get their donation refunded by other taxpayers. Corporations in particular could direct large sums to private education at public expense.
